# Introduction

Prostate cancer (PCa) is the second most prevalent form of cancer among men worldwide accounting for 29.4% of cancer cases and is the fifth leading cause of cancer deaths among men (Bray et al. 2024). In spite of this, PCa screening poses a risk of false-positives with over-diagnosis and over-treatment (look for a citation for this. cochrane review includes ERSPC and PLCO with contradictory results. Goteborg shows positive results of screening. Maybe read the individual studies). Treatment of indolent disease that would have never developed into metastatic disease can cause considerable harms. Therefore, there is a need for more-accurate screening methods to improve the effectiveness of early screening and to reduce the negative consequences of overdiagnosis among men. Furthermore, screening methods should ideally identify individuals at elevated risk of aggressive, metastatic, or clinically-significant prostate cancer for early screening of prostate cancer via PSA and MRI to avoid over-diagnosis and over-treatment of indolent disease.

The heritability of PCa is high, estimated to 42% (cite Lichtenstein), and more than ### common (cite) and rare genetic variants (cite) have been identified. One approach to reduce the false positive rate for early screening and to reduce the risk of harms due to screening is to employ genetic testing to stratify individuals by inherited risk factors. The most common approach to genetic screening for cancer is with rare pathogenic variants (RPVs). For example, women carrying a pathogenic mutation in the BRCA2 gene have a 60% chance of developing breast cancer in their lifetime \[citation\]. There are a number of RPVs associated with increased risk of PCa that are, in some cases, associated with worse prognosis, including BRCA1, BRCA2, and HOXB13 G84E \[cite Tyler's paper\]. For example, carrying a HOXB13 mutation can increase an individual's risk by a factor of 2-6 \[Tyler\]. However, these variants are at relatively low frequency in the general population (typically, 0.05-0.1%) and therefore are of limited use in identifying most individuals with clinically relevant risk, though certain variants, such as HOXB13, are at a higher frequency in Scandinavian populations (1.3%; Seibert).

An alternative approach to screening for RPVs is to use polygenic scores (PGS). In this case, many common genetic variants with small effect sizes may be combined to calculate a score for an individual. Recent work has shown that individuals with high (2-3x) or very high (3.5-9x) risk based on polygenic scores---comparable in magnitude to carrying a single RPV---make up as much as 20-25% of the population (Seibert 2023). Therefore, PGSs can potentially be more useful for identifying more individuals at increased risk of cancer to target for further screening. Furthermore, genotyping is still cheaper than whole-genome sequencing and panel sequencing (define this) and can be used to simultaneously assess the risk for many diseases, not just cancer but also for mental disorders or cardiovascular disease, which potentially makes it a more cost-effective screening procedure than sequencing (probably need some recent citations documenting the cost).

Typical PGS models use case-control designs with logistic regression to calculate a polygenic risk score (PRS) to estimate the risk of developing cancer at any age. More clinically relevant is to predict age of diagnosis or age of onset in a survival modeling framework which makes it possible to estimate the risk of developing disease at an early age (cite Desikan 2017, Seibert 2018). Genetic risk scores using this survival modeling framework are called polygenic hazard scores (PHS) and have been demonstrated to stratify individuals based on predicted age of onset for prostate cancer in multi-ethnic groups (city Seibert, Huynh-Le 2021). Furthermore, PHS can be combined with PSA screening and family history to potentially improve the positive predictive value of these screening measures (Seibert et al. 2018). By stratifying individuals using PHS, we can identify individuals who would benefit most from early PSA screening.

To date, few studies have tested published PHS models in populations that differ from the development set. One example of this was the PHS model of Alzheimer's disease from Desikan et al. (2017), which was tested in novel Nordic cohorts from Norway and Denmark (Motazedi 2023). While several PHS models for PCa age-of-diagnosis have been published (Seibert, others), to our knowledge, none have been externally validated in populations that may have different clinical characteristics, ancestral background, or missing SNPs from the model (check what has/has not been tested in external cohorts. Several exist, but not in Norway and not in these specific cohorts). The earliest models in this area were criticized for being developed in European populations and for not being generalizable to non-European populations. However, more recent PCa PHS models have been developed in more diverse cohorts, such as in the Million Veterans Program in the US, and has been shown to stratify individuals in multi-ethnic populations (Huynh-Le et al., 2021, Seibert, 2025 pre-print).

In this study, we evaluated the latest PHS model for individual-level early diagnosis of PCa by performing external validation in two Norwegian cohorts: the Hordaland Health Studies (Helseundersøkelsene i Hordaland; HUSK) population study and the Norwegian Familial Cancer Study (NFCS), a clinical study enriched for patients with family history of cancer. These two distinct cohorts provide a unique opportunity to evaluate predictive performance of PCa PHS in the general population and in a clincal cohort In addition, we used whole-genome sequencing data from a subset of individuals to identify RPVs, we compared the efficacy of screening using PHS and RPVs. Lastly, we validated whether these models can identify individuals at increased risk of metastatic disease. 

In this study, we tested the PHS601 model in two Norwegian cohorts. This model includes 601 SNPs and was developed in the the United States Veterans Affairs Million Veterans Program and validated in data from the PRACTICAL Consortium and the All of Us Research Program (Vassy et al.). We chose this model because it is the latest published PHS model developed in the largest (585,418) and most diverse cohort. In addition, it is being evaluated in a clinical trial in the VA healthcare system (Clinicaltrials.gov NCT05926102). 

Norway offers a unique opportunity for investigating these questions due to their well-developed electronic health records system, which allows investigators to link patient data from disparate health registries including the cancer registry. Such biobank-linked healthcare systems offer the ideal opportunity to test and implement precision care for individualized risk prediction using genomics. 

# Methods

## Study Population

Two Norwegian cohorts were included in this study. 

The first cohort was the Hordaland Health Studies (Helseundersøkelsene i Hordaland; HUSK). This cohort was recruited from Rogaland county in western Norway in two waves. The first wave was in 1992/1993 and the second wave was in 1997/1999. HUSK participants were genotyped at deCODE Genetics (https://www.decode.com/) in two batches (10,083 and 25,432 individuals in batch 1 and 2, respectively) using customized Illumina GSA v3 array (687316 genotyped variants). Prior to phasing and imputation genotyping data were QCed separately for each batch using plink2. QC steps for variants included removal of indels, non-ATGC, strand ambiguous, poorly genotyped (plink2's option: --geno 0.05), non-autosomal and rare (--maf 0.05) variants as well as variants with extreme deviation from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (--hwe 1E-50 midp keep-fewhet). Chromosomal strand and allele order for the remaining variants were aligned based on the HGDP + 1KG reference panel from gnomAD (https://gnomad.broadinstitute.org/downloads#v3-hgdp-1kg) [PMID: 38749656], and variants with alleles which were not possible to align to the reference as well as variants with MAF deviating from the reference by more than 30% were removed. Resulting genotypes from two batches were merged, variants with high missingness (--geno 0.02) and individuals with poor genotyping rate (--mind 0.05) were removed from the merged data. The combined dataset was then phased and imputed with Beagle 5.4 (version 27May24.118) using the HGDP + 1KG reference panel. [Imputed data were further QCed by removing variants with low imputation quality (Beagle's DR2<0.5) and variants with minor allele frequency below 0.5% (--maf 0.005). The resulting dataset contained 10531075 variants and 35476 individuals.] This may not be true since we used the "raw" data, double check the number of alleles in the full imputation and update the participant count programmatically so it matchces the real count.

The second cohort was the Norwegian Familial Cancer Study (NFCS; Mattingsdal, 2021). Participants in this cohort were recruited in 1980-1995 from all of Norway via self-report based on over-representation of cancer in their families. Genomic DNA was extracted from peripheral blood samples using the DNeasy Blood & Tissue Kit (Qiagen, Germantown, MD, USA), following the manufacturer’s protocol, and analyzed using the Illumina OmniExpress 24 v1.1 chip at deCODE genetics (Reykjavik, Iceland) \[cite Mattingsdal\]. The genotyped dataset consisted of 15,769 participants with 713,014 SNPs. Genotype data were imputed using the HRC v1.1 reference panel (Mattingsdal) following the same imputation protocol as The Norwegian Mother, Father and Child Cohort (MoBa) (https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.06.23.496289v4). After imputation, the dataset consisted of 7,526,252 SNPs. 

## Characterization of PCa Cases

PCa cases were defined as participants with ICD10 code C61. Diagnosis date was the first instance of this ICD10 code in the registry data. Controls were limited to males excluding those censored before age 40, since no diagnoses were observed before that age, and censored at age of last observation and we did not remove individuals with other cancer diagnoses. Metastatic disease was defined as disease that extends to lymph nodes inside or outside the same body region, organ metastasis outside the body region, and microscopic or macroscopic ingrowth into neighboring structures (corresponding to metastasis codes `{r} metastase_strict[1:length(metastase_strict)-1]`, and `{r} metastase_strict[length(metastase_strict)]` in the Norwegian Cancer Registry). 

## Harmonize alleles and calculate PHSes

Three SNPs were removed based on incompatible alleles. The rest had a perfect match without considering strand flips.

Lay out how many SNPs were removed at each stage of the process (those missing due to the harmonize alleles script and those absent from the genotype data.)

 The list of variants used by the model, and their effect sizes, were acquired by contacting the authors. Individual genotype data and model variants were aligned using the cleansumstats pipeline (github link) to harmonize effect and reference alleles as well as chromosome positions and RSIDs to GRCh37 genomic build. This pipeline removed palindromes, indels, and impossible allele pairs. The reference panel for our imputation did not include indels so their removal would not affect the results. After the pipeline, of the initial 601 SNPs in PHS601,  SNPs were removed as palindromes (i.e., ambiguous allele pairs), indels, or impossible allele pairs leaving  SNPs in the model. Of the  SNPs remaining from PHS601,  SNPs were missing from the NFCS genotype data, which meant the PHSes for these participants were calculated from the remaining  SNPs. Likewise SNPs were missing from the HUSK genotype data so the PHSes for these SNPs were calculated from  SNPs remaining from PHS601. Polygenic hazard scores were calculated for each cohort via matrix multiplication. The resulting PHSes were centered and scaled prior to modeling.

## Sequencing and variant calling

Information on number of participants with wgs, sequencing platform, QC, etc. 

Variant calling was performed using the CPSR package \[Nakken et al. 2021\]. We identified individuals with genetic variants from ClinVar that were classified as "pathogenic" including at least one copy of RPVs known to be associated with increased risk of PCa including mutations within the genes ATM, BRCA1, BRCA2, HOXB13, MLH1, MLH2, and MSH6.

## Comparison of cohort incidence rate to the general Norwegian population from the cancer registry

To evaluate how generalizable our results were to the population of Norway, we compared the incidence rate in each cohort for both PCa (any stage) and for metastatic PCa to the predicted annualized incidence rate from the Norwegian cancer registry. Cancer registry data were for PCa cases in Norway for the years 2014-2017 as reported by Huynh-le et al. (2020). First, we fit an exponential model to the average incidence for each 5-year age group. For PCa, the best fit was an exponential quadratic and for metastatic PCa the best fit was an exponential. We then predicted the annualized incidence from this model and calculated the cumulative incidence rate from the cumulative sum of cases. We compared these to the cumulative incidence rates derived from the Cox PH model for each cohort and each phenotype (PCa or metastatic PCa). Given that the NFCS cohort was recruited based on a family history of cancer and that the incidence rate for this cohort displayed a systematically higher risk of PCa than the general population (see @{suppfig-comp}), we chose to focus on the HRs from the models fit to the HUSK data for the following analysis.


## Statistics

Polygenic hazard scores were evaluated in both cohorts using Cox proportional hazards models using the `coxph` function from the `survival` package in `R` (cite). For the any-PCa model, events were defined as age of first PCa diagnosis and controls were censored at age of last observation. For the metastatic PCa model, events were defined as age at first metastatic disease diagnosis. Polygenic hazard scores were centered and scaled prior to model fit. After model fitting, participants were separated by centile range of PHS into the top 20%, the bottom 20%, and the middle 60% for plotting of K-M curves. Performance of each model is reported as HR~SD~, which is the hazard ratio increase for a one-standard-deviation increase in PHS, HR~80/20~, which is the hazard ratio between the top 20% and the bottom 20% of PHS, HR~80/50~, which is the hazard ratio between the top 20% and the median PHS, as well as Harrell's concordance index (C-index). For these metrics, 95% confidence intervals were generated using `{r} bootstrap_iters` bootstrap iterations.

Next we assessed the effect of RPVs on risk predicition. Only the NFCS cohort received WGS so the HUSK cohort was excluded from these analyses. To test whether RPVs were at higher frequency in cases than in controls, we used the one-sided Fisher's exact test. No participants had mutations in two of the genes (MSH2 and MSH6) so these genes were removed prior to analysis. The remaining 5 genes were tested individually as well as aggregated as individuals carrying any of the variants. The p-values from the Fisher's tests were adjusted using the Benjamini & Hochberg correction. The one gene at elevated frequency in the cases (HOXB13) was then used in a Cox survival analysis to estimate the risk of PCa associated with carrying this pathogenic variant. This model was evaluated based on the HR between carriers and non-carriers as well as the C-index. To test whether individuals with high PHS were more likely to carry a rare variant, we used logistic regression. To compare the HOXB13 carriers to PHS, we subgrouped the dataset for individuals with both WGS and genotyping and refit the Cox model of PHS with this smaller sample and calculated the HR for a similar proportion of individuals as were HOXB13 carriers. In this case, 1.7% of participants carried a HOXB13 mutation so we calculated the HR between the top 1.7% of PHSes and the median subject.  

All Cox models were evaluated for the proportional hazards assumption using the `cox.zph` and by inspecting plots of the Schoenfeld residuals versus time via `plot.cox.zph` (Cite Grambsch and Therneau 1994 Biometrika). Coefficients that violated the proportionality assumption were refit with time-dependendent covariates. In each case, the decline in HR was roughly linear so we used a linear time transform (i.e., PHS $\cdot$ age) for the time-dependent PHS with the `tt` function. 

# Results

## PHS601 accurately stratifies Norwegian cohorts based on PCa risk

We first tested the performance of PHS601 in stratifying participants based on risk of PCa diagnosis (any stage) in two Norwegian cohorts. In the HUSK cohort, there were `{r} p2521_sample_size[1, 3]` individuals with a PCa diagnosis and `{r} format(p2521_sample_size[[1, 4]], scientific = FALSE)` controls. The Cox proportional hazards model showed an `r (round(p2521_PHS601[1, 3], 2) * 100) - 100`\% greater risk of PCa for a one-standard-deviation increase in PHS (HR~SD~ = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_PHS601[1, "value"], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_PHS601[1, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_PHS601[1, "conf.high"], 2))`]; @{tbl-1}). Individuals with PHS in the top quintile had over `{r} floor(p2521_PHS601[2, 3])` times greater risk of PCa than individuals in the bottom quintile (HR~80/20~: `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_PHS601[2, 3], 2))`, 95\% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_PHS601[2, 4], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_PHS601[2, 5], 2))`\]) and `{r} (round(p2521_PHS601[4, 3], 2) * 100) - 100`\% greater risk than the median individual (HR~80/50~: `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_PHS601[4, 3], 2))`, 95\% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_PHS601[4, 4], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_PHS601[4, 5], 2))`\]; @{fig-phs}A).

The proportionality test and plot of weighted residuals revealed a negative trend in HR with age suggesting that the proportionality assumption was invalid for PHS and that the risk associated with PHS was age-dependent (Chi. sq. = `r round(p2521_zph[1, "chisq"], 2)`, df = `r p2521_zph[1, "df"]`, p = `r pvalr(p2521_zph[1, "p"])`). The effect size seemed to decrease roughly linearly with age, so we refit the model as an extended Cox model with a time-dependent PHS covariate with a linear time transform and a y-intercept at age 40. In this model, there was a `r p2521_coxph_results %>% filter(model == "phs_tt" & term == "phs") %>% pull(estimate) %>% sprintf("%.1f", .)` times greater risk for a one-standard-deviation increase in PHS at age 40 (HR~SD~ = `r p2521_coxph_results %>% filter(model == "phs_tt" & term == "phs") %>% pull(estimate) %>% sprintf("%.2f", .)`, 95% CI [`r p2521_coxph_results %>% filter(model == "phs_tt" & term == "phs") %>% pull(conf.low) %>% round(2) %>% sprintf("%.2f", .)`, `r p2521_coxph_results %>% filter(model == "phs_tt" & term == "phs") %>% pull(conf.high) %>% round(2) %>% sprintf("%.2f", .)`], p `r p2521_coxph_results %>% filter(model == "phs_tt" & term == "phs") %>% pull(p.value) %>% pvalr()`), which declined by `r round(1 - p2521_coxph_results[4, "estimate"], 3) * 100`\% per year (HR = `{r} sprintf("%.3f", round(p2521_coxph_results[4, "estimate"], 3))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_coxph_results[4, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_coxph_results[4, "conf.high"], 2))`], p = `{r} pvalr(p2521_coxph_results[4, "p.value"])`). However, the time varying effect size was weak, and the weighted residual plot showed high variability in the time-varying coefficient. Therefore, in the previous paragraph and in @{fig-phs}A we have presented the Cox model without the time-transformed PHS.

In the NFCS cohort, there were `{r} p212_sample_size[1, 3]` individuals with a PCa diagnosis and `{r} p212_sample_size[1, 4]` controls. The Cox proportional hazards model showed a `r (round(p212_PHS601[1, 3], 2) * 100) - 100`\% greater risk of PCa for a one-standard-deviation increase in PHS (HR~SD~ = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_PHS601[1, "value"], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_PHS601[1, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_PHS601[1, "conf.high"], 2))`]; @{tbl-1}). Individuals with PHS in the top quintile had over `{r} floor(p212_PHS601[2, 3])` times greater risk of any PCa than individuals in the bottom quintile (HR~80/20~: `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_PHS601[2, 3], 2))`, 95\% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_PHS601[2, 4], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_PHS601[2, 5], 2))`\]) and `{r} (round(p212_PHS601[4, 3], 2) * 100) - 100`\% greater risk than the median individual (HR~80/50~: `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_PHS601[4, 3], 2))`, 95\% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_PHS601[4, 4], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_PHS601[4, 5], 2))`\]; @{fig-phs}B).

Similar to the HUSK cohort, in the NFCS cohort, the proportionality test and plot of weighted residuals revealed a negative trend in HR with age (Chi. sq. = `r round(p212_zph[1, "chisq"], 2)`, df = `r p212_zph[1, "df"]`, p = `r pvalr(p212_zph[1, "p"])`). We again fit the model as an extended Cox model with a time-dependent PHS covariate with a linear time transform and a y-intercept at age 40. In this model, there was a `r p212_coxph_results %>% filter(model == "phs_tt" & term == "phs") %>% pull(estimate) %>% round(2) * 100 - 100`\% increase in risk for a one-standard-deviation increase in PHS at age 40 (HR~SD~ = `r p212_coxph_results %>% filter(model == "phs_tt" & term == "phs") %>% pull(estimate) %>% sprintf("%.2f", .)`, 95% CI [`r p212_coxph_results %>% filter(model == "phs_tt" & term == "phs") %>% pull(conf.low) %>% round(2) %>% sprintf("%.2f", .)`, `r p212_coxph_results %>% filter(model == "phs_tt" & term == "phs") %>% pull(conf.high) %>% round(2) %>% sprintf("%.2f", .)`], p `r p212_coxph_results %>% filter(model == "phs_tt" & term == "phs") %>% pull(p.value) %>% pvalr()`), which declined by `r round(1 - p212_coxph_results[4, "estimate"], 3) * 100`\% per year (HR = `{r} sprintf("%.3f", round(p212_coxph_results[4, "estimate"], 3))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_coxph_results[4, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_coxph_results[4, "conf.high"], 2))`], p = `{r} pvalr(p212_coxph_results[4, "p.value"])`). However, the time varying effect size was weak and the weighted residual plot showed high variability in the time-varying coefficient. Therefore, in the previous paragraph and in @{fig-phs}B we have presented the Cox model without the time-transformed PHS.

## PHS601 associated with metastatic PCa in Norwegian cohorts

In addition to evaluating the performance of PHS601 in stratifying individuals based on risk of PCa at any stage, we were also interested in the association of PHS601 with metastatic disease. In the HUSK cohort, `{r} p2521_sample_size[2, 3]` individuals had been diagnosed with metastatic disease leaving `{r} format(p2521_sample_size[[2, 4]], scientific = FALSE)` controls. The Cox proportional hazards model of metastatic disease showed a `{r} (round(p2521_PHS601_meta[1, "value"], 2) * 100) - 100`\% greater risk of metastatic disease for a one-standard-deviation increase in PHS (HR~SD~ = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_PHS601_meta[1, "value"], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_PHS601_meta[1, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_PHS601_meta[1, "conf.high"], 2))`]; @{tbl-1}). Individuals with PHS in the top quintile had over `{r} floor(p2521_PHS601_meta[2, 3])` times greater risk of metastatic disease than individuals in the bottom quintile (HR~80/20~: `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_PHS601_meta[2, 3], 2))`, 95% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_PHS601_meta[2, 4], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_PHS601_meta[2, 5], 2))`\]) and `{r} (round(p2521_PHS601_meta[4, 3], 2) * 100) - 100`\% greater risk than the median individual (HR~80/50~: `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_PHS601_meta[4, 3], 2))`, 95% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_PHS601_meta[4, 4], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_PHS601_meta[4, 5], 2))`\]; @{fig-meta}A)

In the NFCS cohort, `{r} p212_sample_size[2, 3]` individuals had been diagnosed with metastatic disease leaving `{r} p212_sample_size[2, 4]` controls. The Cox proportional hazards model of metastatic disease showed a `{r} (round(p212_PHS601_meta[1, "value"], 2) * 100) - 100`\% greater risk of metastatic disease for a one-standard-deviation increase in PHS (HR~SD~ = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_PHS601_meta[1, "value"], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_PHS601_meta[1, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_PHS601_meta[1, "conf.high"], 2))`]; @{tbl-1}). Individuals with PHS in the top quintile had over `{r} floor(p212_PHS601_meta[2, 3])` times greater risk of metastatic disease than individuals in the bottom quintile (HR~80/20~: `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_PHS601_meta[2, 3], 2))`, 95% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_PHS601_meta[2, 4], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_PHS601_meta[2, 5], 2))`\]) and `{r} (round(p212_PHS601_meta[4, 3], 2) * 100) - 100`\% greater risk than the median individual (HR~80/50~: `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_PHS601_meta[4, 3], 2))`, 95% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_PHS601_meta[4, 4], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_PHS601_meta[4, 5], 2))`\]; @{fig-meta}B)

## PHS and HOXB13 independently contribute to increased PCa risk in the NFCS cohort

We next compared the performance of RPVs and PHSes in predicting risk of PCa (any stage). Only the NFCS cohort received WGS so the HUSK cohort was excluded from these analyses. We first subsetted our dataset to include only participants that received both WGS and genotyping. We then re-analyzed the PHS data on this smaller subsample to compare it to the performance of the RPVs. There were a total of `{r} wgs_summary[2]` participants with WGS of which `{r} wgs_summary[1]` were cases and `{r} wgs_summary[2] - wgs_summary[1]` were controls. Among these individuals, a total of `{r} wgs_summary[10]` had a predisposing mutation in one of the seven genes that we investigated: BRCA1, BRCA2, HOXB13, MLH1, ATM, MSH2, and MSH6. No participants were observed with mutations in MSH2 or MSH6 so these genes were removed from the analysis.

As a preliminary analysis, we tested whether the frequency of mutations was greater in cases than in controls for each gene using a one-sided Fisher's exact test. Only the HOXB13 gene showed increased frequency in the cases when compared to the controls (OR = `r sprintf("%.2f", round(fisher[2, "estimate"], 2))`, 95% lower confidence bound = `r sprintf("%.2f", round(fisher[2, "conf.low"], 2))`, adj. p = `{r} pvalr(fisher[2, "p.adjust"], digits = 2)`). Therefore, we only proceeded with testing the risk of diagnosis with this gene. HOXB13 gene mutations were at a frequency of `r round(wgs_summary$hoxb13_carrier_1 / wgs_summary$wgs_1 * 100, 1)`\% in the WGS subsample and having a high polygenic score was associated with being more likely to carry a rare variant (OR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(binomial_phs_hoxb13[2, "estimate"], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(binomial_phs_hoxb13[2, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(binomial_phs_hoxb13[2, "conf.high"], 2))`], p = `{r} pvalr(binomial_phs_hoxb13[[2, "p.value"]])`).

Using the subsetted WGS sample, the Cox proportional hazards model for PHS showed a `{r} (round(wgs_phs[1, "value"], 2) * 100) - 100`\% greater risk of PCa for a one-standard-deviation increase in PHS (HR~SD~ = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_phs[1, "value"], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_phs[1, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_phs[1, "conf.high"], 2))`]). Individuals with PHS in the top quintile had over `{r} floor(wgs_phs[2, 3])` times greater risk of any PCa than individuals in the bottom quintile (HR~80/20~: `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_phs[2, 3], 2))`, 95\% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_phs[2, 4], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_phs[2, 5], 2))`\]) and `{r} (round(wgs_phs[4, 3], 2) * 100) - 100`\% greater risk than the median individual (HR~80/50~: `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_phs[4, 3], 2))`, 95\% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_phs[4, 4], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_phs[4, 5], 2))`\]; @{fig-hoxb13}A). By comparison, the Cox proportional hazards model for HOXB13 carriers showed a `{r} round(wgs_hoxb13[1, "value"], 1)` times greater risk of PCa for carriers of HOXB13 mutations than non-carriers (HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_hoxb13[1, "value"], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_hoxb13[1, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_hoxb13[1, "conf.high"], 2))`]; @{fig-hoxb13}B). 

Combining these two predictors into a single Cox model, we found that both PHS and HOXB13 carrier status can independently contribute to increased PCa risk. In the combined main effect model, a one-standard-deviation increase in PHS led to a `{r} (round(wgs_results[3, 2], 2) * 100) - 100`\% increase in PCa risk (HR~SD~ = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[3, "estimate"], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[3, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[3, "conf.high"], 2))`], p `{r} pvalr(wgs_results[[3, "p.value"]])`) while carrying a HOXB13 mutation increased risk by `{r} (round(wgs_results[4, 2], 2) * 100) - 100`\% `{r} round(wgs_results[4, 2], 1)` times (HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[4, "estimate"], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[4, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[4, "conf.high"], 2))`], p = `{r} pvalr(wgs_results[[4, "p.value"]])`). The interaction term was not significant (HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[7, "estimate"], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[7, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[7, "conf.high"], 2))`], p = `{r} pvalr(wgs_results[[7, "p.value"]])`), therefore we have presented only the main effect model here. 

To compare the PHS and HOXB13 models directly, we calculated the PHS HR for a similar proportion of the population as are HOXB13 carriers. Since 1.7% of participants carried a HOXB13 mutation, we calculated the HR between the top 1.7% of PHSes and the median PHS and found that someone in the top 1.7% of PHSes had a `{r} round(wgs_phs_95[[1, "value"]], 2)` times greater risk of PCa than the median individual (HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_phs_95[[1, "value"]], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_phs_95[[1, "conf.low"]], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_phs_95[[1, "conf.high"]], 2))`]). By comparison, a HOXB13 carrier had a `{r} round(wgs_hoxb13[[1, "value"]], 2)` times greater risk of PCa than a non-carrier (HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_hoxb13[[1, "value"]], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_hoxb13[[1, "conf.low"]], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_hoxb13[[1, "conf.high"]], 2))`]).


## Predicting population risk of prostate cancer onset based on HR from the HUSK cohort

Finally, we looked at the predicted risk stratification for PCa in the general population based on the HRs from our PHS models. Here, we used the exponential models that we fit to the data from Huynh-Le et al. (2020) as the population baseline incidence rate. We then stratified these curves by the HR for the top 20% and bottom 20% of PHSes from the Cox PH model fit to the HUSK cohort data as reported in @{tbl-1}. We performed this separately for any-stage PCa and for metastatic PCa (@{fig-strat}).

Change this to be cumulative rather than instantaneous risk

Based on an individual's age and PHS, we can see their instantaneous risk for developing PCa within the next year in @{fig-strat}A. For example, a healthy (i.e., cancer-free) individual at age 75 who is in the top 80% of PHSes has about a 1.5% risk compared to someone in the bottom 20% who has about a 0.75% risk. There is a considerably higher predicted incidence rate for individuals with PHS in the top quintile than the baseline with around 50% more cases in this quintile than in the baseline at age 75. It is important to note that the decline in incidence rate after 70 in @{fig-strat}A in is likely an artifact of reduced screening rather than a real decrease in incidence rate (cite Hunhy-Le 2020).

# Discussion

We observed strong stratification in both Norwegian cohorts, which demonstrates the potential of PHS601 in a precision screen paradigm in Norway. The strong stratification in the HUSK cohort demonstrates good risk stratification in the general population. In addition, the NFCS cohort was recruited based on self-reported family history of cancer and showed elevated cancer-risk relative to the general Norwegian population (@{suppfig-comp}). Given the strong risk stratification in this group, this suggests that genetics in this model is not just a proxy for family history (You need to clarify this sentence).

For metastatic disease, we also found good stratification between high- and low-risk individuals based on PHS. In the NFCS cohort, the effect was only marginally significant with the 99% confidence intervals for the HR barely overlapping 1.00. However, we show a similar magnitude effect with greater confidence in the HUSK cohort. This suggests PHS601 could be effective at identifying individuals at greater risk of metastatic disease and therefore with the greatest clinical benefit for further screening via PSA or imaging.

In addition to testing the general performance of PHS, we also compared PHS to screening for RPVs such as HOXB13. Even in the case of low sample sizes, for example, in the NFCS cohort, we had only `{r} p212_sample_size[1, 3]` cases of prostatic cancer and `{r} p212_sample_size[2, 3]` cases of metastatic disease, the polygenic score was more useful than identifying RPVs in the same sample size. In addition, genotyping for polygenic scoring costs a fraction of sequencing (source? numbers on this?). A much larger percentage of the population are affected by a high risk score than are affected by currently known PRVs. High polygenic risk affects 50x more people than BRCA2 mutations, which means genetic risk scoring may be more useful for more people. If someone is a carrier of a pathogenic mutation in BRCA2 or HOXB13, that tells you they have a relatively high risk of developing cancer, however, it provides no information about the relative risk of patients without those rare variants. Whereas, a polygenic risk score can inform risk in all patients. Evaluating how this could work in Norway, there is more value per NOK for PHS screening than for sequencing. PHS has a potentially larger public health benefit.

The combined Cox model with both PHS and HOXB13 was also significant, which suggests that both polygenic score as well as rare deleterious mutations contribute independently to PCa risk. As we show, having a high PHS score does not appear to predict being a carrier of HOXB13 G84E. Therefore, both of these genetic factors can provide valuable information about individual risk. It is possible that clinical interventions differ between individuals whose phenotype arises from rare deleterious mutations and individuals whose phenotype arises from the interaction of environment with genotype of the normal array of segregating genes of minor effect. Furthermore, RPVs and PHSes have different implications for genetic counseling for example, for the risk of offspring being affected in the case of RPVs.

While the time varying effect of PHS was weak, we did see a significant negative trend in the HR of PHS with age in two independent cohorts such that the strongest effect of genetic risk was at the youngest ages (40s). This has a couple of implications. First, the genetic risk stratification appears to be the strongest at younger ages (at least with the portion of genetic variation captured by this model) and, in fact, would be stronger than the model suggests averaged across all ages. For example, in the HUSK cohort, the HR for any PCa was 1.54, whereas in the time transformed model the HR at age 40 was 1.87. From a utility perspective, this is valuable because we want to identify individuals at risk of early diagnosis who might benefit the most from modifying their risk through lifestyle interventions, pharmaceuticals, or early screening. Second, this suggests that the impact of genetics decreases with age such that congenital risk is greatest in younger individuals and that factors other than genetics, such as lifestyle, have a greater influence in older participants. Future modeling efforts could investigate adding a time-varying component to PHS models to further improve risk stratification based on age and genetic risk.

Future Directions

- Develop a model with Norwegian-specific SNPs. Possible with a larger sample size, perhaps through federated learning using multiple Norwegian cohorts.
- Cost-benefit analysis for genetic cancer screening (compare the cost of genotyping all individuals including the biobank infrastructure to the price per QALY.)
- In our dataset, we did not have access to family history data or prostate-specific antigen measurements. Future studies should expand on this model by including these other factors... should people with high risk score be selected for PSA screening and then PSA added to the risk prediction?

One limitation of this study is the limited sample size of participants with diagnosis data, age of diagnosis, and metastasis code. If we could get a bigger data set, we could potentially identify additional SNPs specific to the Norwegian population.

While information on metastatic or aggressive disease is often lacking in study populations and sample sizes for metastatic disease are relatively small resulting in decreased power, advances in electronic health records systems and biobanks could improve the sample sizes and information necessary to identify individuals with metastatic disease. Therefore, future studies should develop models that are specific to the development of metastatic or aggressive disease

The benefit of using PHS for screening is that a clinician can identify how likely a patient is to develop disease and how likely they are to develop agressive/metastatic/clinically significant disease. This should be determine before deciding whether to measure PSA.
